547	**Changes:**
548	- source.RunOptions gains Offline beside Cache, settled once at Registry.NewResolver so a run is offline for every kind or none; its doc records why failing is the point (skipping, reporting unchanged, or serving whatever commit is cached each turn a run that could not do what it was asked into one that reports success)
549	- The github archive memo turns a cache miss into a kind-neutral errNotCached instead of a fetch when offline, remembered like any other retrieval failure so a second asset of one repository is not made to wait for the same nothing, and wrapped per caller so each asset's diagnostic names itself
550	- Ref resolution branches above the lookup rather than inside it: resolveRefOffline resolves a full commit identifier exactly as an online run does and refuses a tag, branch or absent ref outright, so no `git ls-remote` runs at all
551	- Two diagnostics: OfflineRefError, separate from UnknownRefError because the ref is not known to be wrong, and OfflineArchiveError, separate from ArchiveRetrievalError because nothing was asked so there is no host or status to quote and the remedy is a networked run rather than a manifest edit
552	- describeRef extracted from RefLookupError into one package function both offline and lookup diagnostics use, so an absent ref is never described two ways
553	- newKind now takes source.RunOptions rather than a bare cache, so a field added to the run's options reaches the kind without another parameter; ~12 test call sites moved with it
554	- offline_internal_test.go covers the four spec scenarios: a cached commit resolving with no request of any kind, an uncached commit naming asset/repository/commit, every uncached asset named rather than the first, four ref shapes refused with the runner failing the test if called, offline plus the cache bypass resolving nothing, and an online run still reaching both git and the forge
555	- CLAUDE.md gains "An offline run refuses a name, and refuses it without asking", and the two new diagnostics are added to both declared failure lists in errors_test.go
556	
557	**Learnings:**
558	- The spec's "a branch or tag with no cached resolution" has no producer at the source layer: nothing records ref→commit until section 9's lockfile. The honest implementation is that only a full commit identifier resolves offline — and that costs nothing later, because the lockfile's recorded commit *is* a commit identifier, so task 10.15 is wiring rather than a second offline path.
559	- The offline branch has to sit above resolveRef rather than inside it. A gitRunner that refused would satisfy "no network request" while violating "no ref lookup is attempted", and would produce the wrong diagnostic — the failure would render as a lookup that failed rather than as one that was never made.
560	- Vacuity-checking both branches was worth it and only half-confirmed what was expected: disabling the offline archive branch failed three tests, disabling the ref branch failed the four ref-shape cases — but the fully-cached positive test passes either way, because a cache hit and a commit-identifier ref both short-circuit ahead of the offline check. A positive offline test can only ever assert the absence of a request, never the presence of the offline branch.
561	- An offline miss must be checked before the status classification in retrievalFailure: errNotCached carries no *source.StatusError, so ordering is not load-bearing for correctness today, but a sentinel that reached the ArchiveRetrievalError branch would render "could not retrieve ... : this machine has no cached archive" — a message about a retrieval that never happened.
562	- Widening newKind from a bare cache to source.RunOptions is what makes the next option free: iteration 23 predicted offline would be "a second field consumed at the same two sites", and that only held for New/Registry — the unexported constructor still needed the widening, so the prediction was right about the design and wrong about the diff.
563	
564	### Iteration 25
565	
566	**Summary:** Implemented the `local` source kind of the add-harnaas-install change — reads anchored at `.harnaas`, identical offline resolution, and the missing/escaping/unreadable diagnostics (tasks 4.1–4.2, 22/122 → 24/122) with fmt, lint and the full test suite clean.
567	
568	**Changes:**
569	- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/local is the new kind package: it accepts source.RunOptions and deliberately ignores them, because a local read makes no request — so an offline run and a networked one do identical work and the cache has nothing to offer a read costing one syscall, which is the spec's 'local sources still resolve offline' scenario satisfied structurally rather than by a branch
570	- Every read goes through a handle anchored at `.harnaas` (os.OpenRoot), so containment is the kernel's answer at the moment of the read rather than harnaas's at the moment of the check — the mirror of archive extraction's textual containment, which is textual because an archive already in hand has no filesystem to race with
571	- Both accepted spellings resolve through one path: the project-local form carries the whole path on the asset, the keyed form splits it between a `local:` sources entry and a path within it, and joining them once leaves every read indifferent to which the author used; a single file resolves under its own leaf name, matching archive extraction's rule
572	- The walk follows a link only at the asset's own path, where the anchor bounds where it can lead, and refuses one inside the tree as an entry harnaas cannot install — the rule the archive kind already applies, and additionally what makes the walk unable to loop on a link back up the tree
573	- Five diagnostics in the {problem, fix} shape, each naming the asset and the path relative to the *project root* in the manifest's own spelling: MissingSourceError (a project with no .harnaas at all reports the asset's own path, not the directory), EmptySourceError (a directory somebody created and left empty is not the same mistake as one nobody created), ContainmentError, UnsupportedEntryError and ReadError
574	- Provenance for a local source records the kind and the source spelled the way the manifest declares it, and claims no ref, commit or mutability — a local source pins nothing, and whether the bytes changed is the digests' question
575	- Test coverage across an external suite (file and directory shapes, the keyed form, provenance, offline resolving identically to online, missing source, absent .harnaas, empty directory, byte-for-byte content including CRLF and a NUL, the declared-failure-list contract) and an internal suite for the escape classification driven by a real anchored handle
576	- CLAUDE.md gains 'A local source is read through a handle, and asks nobody anything', recording why the kind ignores the run options, why containment is kernel-enforced here and textual in the archive, why three refusals are told apart, and why the message match is safe
577	
578	**Learnings:**
579	- os does not export the sentinel behind a Root's 'path escapes from parent' refusal — os.ErrPathEscapes exists only in the standard library's own export_test.go — so distinguishing an escape from a not-exist and from a permission failure can only be done by matching the message. The fallback is what makes it safe: a rewording reports the containment violation as a read that failed, which is less specific, never wrong, and never lets the read through. Same trade iteration 8 made for encoding/json's unknown-field message.
580	- os.Symlink fails for an unprivileged Windows user ('A required privilege is not held by the client'), so the two symlink-driven scenarios can only skip on this machine. A `..` component produces the *same* refusal from the same standard-library code with no privilege at all, which is what makes the classification assertable on every platform — worth reaching for even though `..` is unreachable through a manifest, because the grammar strips it long before a read.
581	- Following symlinks during a directory walk is a loop hazard a visited-set cannot catch: a link back up the tree generates an ever-longer path, so each Stat is a fresh path and only a depth bound or a refusal stops it. Refusing a link inside the selected subtree — which is already the archive kind's rule — removes the hazard without inventing a limit nobody asked for.
582	- os.Root gained FS() in Go 1.25 returning an fs.FS that implements ReadDirFS/StatFS/ReadFileFS/ReadLinkFS, so `fs.ReadDir(root.FS(), dir)` is the way to enumerate through an anchored handle — Root itself has ReadFile, Stat and Lstat but no ReadDir.
583	- The local kind is the first source kind to need the project root, and paths.ProjectRoot(ctx) is the sanctioned reader, so it needs no seam of its own: a test passes paths.WithProjectRoot over a t.TempDir. That is cheaper than the parameterized constructors the github kind needed, because there is nothing to stub — no git, no network, no token.
584	- No size ceiling was added for local reads, deliberately: the spec states ceilings only for archive extraction, and section 8.10 enforces hard limits against *rendered* output. A future iteration wanting one would have to export the per-file and per-asset constants that are currently unexported in package source.
585	- revive's context-as-argument rule fires on a test helper spelled `func f(tb testing.TB, ctx context.Context, ...)` — the allowed-types-before default covers *testing.T, not testing.TB. Dropping tb from a helper that only needed it for Helper() is cheaper than configuring the linter.
586	
587	### Iteration 26
588	
589	**Summary:** Implemented source-kind self-registration and the whole source-verification phase of the add-harnaas-install change — shape verification per asset type, a non-re-serializing frontmatter reader and skill name-match refusal (tasks 1.5 and 4.3–4.5, 24/122 → 28/122) with fmt, lint, the full test suite and the e2e suite clean.
590	
591	**Changes:**
592	- The github and local kind packages register themselves with source.Default from their own init (with a named gochecknoinits suppression), and cmd/harnaas/cli/sourcekinds.go is the single reviewed file that links them — so whether harnaas can resolve a kind is whether the binary links its package rather than whether somebody remembered to add it to a list elsewhere
593	- cmd/harnaas/cli/sourcekinds_test.go asserts the v1 set whole rather than by membership (a kind that stopped registering is a manifest that suddenly fails to install; one that started registering is a source form accepted before anybody specified it) and separately proves every registered constructor builds for a run
594	- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/verify.go adds source.Verify, one shape-and-naming check sitting above the kinds because a skill fetched from a forge and one read out of .harnaas are wrong in the same ways: a skill must be a directory carrying SKILL.md, every other type one regular file
595	- Whether a source was a file is derived from the resolved file set rather than carried out of extraction — both kinds resolve a single file under its own leaf name, so one file whose path is the leaf of the declared subtree is a file — which keeps the shape a property every kind already agrees on instead of a flag each kind sets; the one blind spot (a directory holding exactly one file named after itself) is documented and refused either way
596	- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/frontmatter.go adds source.Frontmatter: SplitFrontmatter separates the block textually (LF and CRLF, closing delimiter matched as a whole line so a Markdown rule cannot extend the block) and Decode reads values out of it into the caller's own struct. The type offers no encoder at all, so frontmatter pass-through is structural rather than a rule someone has to remember
597	- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/verify_errors.go adds four {problem, fix} diagnostics: ShapeError carrying expected and found as text, MissingSkillFileError (separate because the edit is in the content, not the manifest), SkillFrontmatterError folding absent/unterminated/unparseable/nameless into one type with four reasons, and SkillNameMismatchError reporting both the installed id and the declared name
598	- Test coverage across frontmatter_test.go (split, CRLF, four no-block spellings, the horizontal-rule case, empty block, unknown fields ignored, invalid YAML, and the block kept byte-for-byte) and verify_test.go (a clean skill, verification rewriting nothing, both skill shape failures, every non-skill type held to the single-file shape in both directions, the one-file directory count, the name mismatch, all four frontmatter reasons, and the problem-then-fix contract)
599	- gopkg.in/yaml.v3 promoted from an indirect to a direct dependency, with the go-licenses gate confirming no new transitive licence
600	- CLAUDE.md gains 'What resolved is verified once, above the kinds, and never rewritten' and a paragraph in the registry section on self-registration and the whole-set assertion
601	
602	**Learnings:**
603	- Shape verification needed 'was this a file or a directory?', and threading that honestly would have widened ExtractSubtree to three returns, NewResolved to three parameters and ~38 call sites. Deriving it instead from (declared subtree leaf, resolved file set) costs one documented blind spot — a directory holding exactly one file named after the directory — and that case is refused either way, only with the wrong one of two shape words. Worth preferring, but the blind spot has to be stated in the code rather than discovered later.
604	- revive's blank-imports rule is not satisfied by a doc comment above the import block: it wants a comment adjacent to each blank import line. gochecknoinits is enabled everywhere except e2e/, so the self-registration the design calls for needs a nolint with a reason in each kind package — which is the right outcome, since it makes the one deliberate exception to harnaas's no-init rule visible in review.
605	- gopkg.in/yaml.v3 was already in the module graph as an indirect dependency via testify, so the planned 'YAML frontmatter parser' dependency cost nothing: go mod edit -require plus go mod tidy left go.sum untouched and the licence gate green.
606	- A frontmatter reader that offers no encoder is a stronger guarantee than a rule about not rewriting. Keeping Raw and Body as the bytes they arrived as and exposing only Decode(v any) means no later phase can re-serialize an author's YAML by accident — which is the real risk for a rule's paths: list, where quoting and folding are a writer's choice and change meaning.
607	- The closing frontmatter delimiter has to match a whole line, not a prefix: a body beginning with a Markdown horizontal rule (----) would otherwise close or extend the block. That case is common enough in real skills to be worth its own test.
608	- Section 4 is complete and source.Verify has no caller yet — the install flow (section 8) is what will call it, the same situation manifest.Interpret was in at the end of the foundation change. Section 5 (the harness adapter contract and registry) is the next unit, and 5.3/5.4 reuse exactly the init-registration and duplicate-panic pattern task 1.5 just wired for source kinds.
609	
610	### Iteration 27
611	
612	**Summary:** Added the harness adapter contract and registry of the add-harnaas-install change — the uniform destination contract with "no surface" as a returned value, self-registration, deterministic listing, duplicate-registration panic and the no-adapter diagnostic (tasks 5.1–5.4, 28/122 → 32/122) with fmt, lint, the full test suite and the e2e suite clean.
613	
614	**Changes:**
615	- cmd/harnaas/cli/adapter is the new contract package: it earns its own package the way source does — the install flow in the flat cli package must import the adapters, so a contract living beside the flow would be a cycle one file later, and separating it is what makes the import boundary of task 5.11 checkable at all
616	- The Adapter contract is four questions and no I/O: the harness it registers under, detection through an fs.FS (so 'detection creates nothing' is a property of the signature rather than a rule each adapter honours), a root per scope returned relative to the scope's own root, and a destination per asset relative to the resolved scope root — so one mapping serves both scopes and the path the lockfile records means the same thing on another machine
617	- A harness with no surface for an asset type is answered as a value rather than mapped to an invented path, because once written a guessed destination is indistinguishable from a real one; the caller reports the pairing unsupported and installs the asset's other targets
618	- Destination carries the surface's terms with its path — support tier, the replacement for a removed surface, the gated or legacy note, and the renderer — so a caller cannot obtain a path and write it without having been told whether the harness still reads there; the renderer is a name rather than a function, which keeps the rendering layer outside the adapter import boundary and lets a surface declare a renderer nobody has written yet
619	- adapter.Tier declares live, gated, legacy and removed with the reason each exists (a harness that has moved on from a path does not say so), and adapter.Renderer declares the two v1 names, identity and as-skill
620	- adapter.Registry mirrors the source registry with one deliberate difference: an adapter is registered as a value rather than as a constructor, because a source kind remembers which archives a run fetched and an adapter is a pure mapping with nothing to remember; Default is the registry adapter packages register into from their own init, and a second adapter for one harness panics
621	- Registry.Lookup returns a typed NotRegisteredError naming the harness and listing those with adapters, phrased for the real situation — the manifest already accepted the name, and a harness with no adapter still receives every shared asset — with Registry.Registered beside it for the flow that asks membership before it has an asset to attribute the answer to
622	- Test coverage across two external files: the destination contract exercised through a claude-code-shaped fake (scope-relative destination, absence returning a zero Destination, an unoffered scope having neither root nor destination, detection reporting absence rather than failure, terms travelling with the path) and the registry (lookup, the no-adapter diagnostic in both the populated and empty forms, its problem-then-fix shape, the duplicate panic, sorted listing independent of registration order, and the package-level Register proven to reach Default)
623	- CLAUDE.md gains 'An adapter answers where, and the absence of an answer is one of the answers', recording why most harnesses need no adapter, why an adapter performs no I/O and returns relative roots, why a missing surface is a value, and why registration takes a value where source takes a constructor
624	
625	**Learnings:**
626	- The spec's 'scope root' is the harness's own directory for that scope (<project>/.claude or ~/.claude), not the project root or the home directory — 'Beneath the resolved scope root, map a rule to rules/<id>.md' settles it. That fixes three things at once: Root(scope) is relative and joined by the caller, Destination.Path is relative to the resolved root so it is identical at both scopes, and task 5.8's containment handle anchors at the harness directory rather than at somebody's whole home.
627	- Making Detect take an fs.FS rather than a directory path turns 'detection has no side effects' into a property of the signature — an fs.FS offers no way to write — and it keeps adapter packages free of os entirely, which will make task 5.11's import allowlist much narrower than it would otherwise have been. os.DirFS implements fs.ReadLinkFS since Go 1.25, so init's deliberate Lstat-not-Stat rule survives the change to fs.
628	- Registering adapters as values rather than as constructors is the right divergence from source.Registry, and the reason is worth stating in code: source.NewKind exists because a kind memoizes a run's archive fetches, and an adapter has nothing to remember. Copying the constructor form would have implied per-run state and forced every future adapter to have a constructor for no reason.
629	- A 'no adapter for this harness' lookup failure is not the same class of error as harness.UnknownError from the roster: the roster question is 'does harnaas know this harness' and the registry question is 'can harnaas install a rule for it'. Both are typed and both list alternatives, but conflating them would tell an author to fix a name that is already correct.
630	- revive's exported rule only reports a stutter when the type name is strictly longer than the package name, so adapter.Adapter is accepted exactly as harness.Harness already is — worth knowing before renaming a type to dodge a warning that never fires.
631	- Section 5's remaining tasks split along what they need: 5.5–5.7 (scope resolution) need only the contract that now exists plus manifest.ResolveScope, which already refuses user scope where the roster records no per-user location, so the adapter layer's job is to not re-implement it; 5.8–5.10 need the install flow's write path; and 5.11's AST boundary test needs at least one adapter package to parse, so it lands with 6.5 rather than before it.
632	
633	### Iteration 28
634	
635	**Summary:** Implemented adapter-layer scope resolution for the add-harnaas-install change — the adapter's own root per scope, the no-silent-fallback refusal naming asset and harness, and the confirmation that the instruction-at-user-scope rule is not restated (tasks 5.5–5.7, 32/122 → 35/122) with fmt, lint, the full test suite and the e2e suite clean.
636	
637	**Changes:**
638	- cmd/harnaas/cli/adapter/scope.go adds ResolveRoot(Adapter, manifest.Asset), which turns an asset's scope into the harness directory it installs beneath, relative to that scope's own root — and takes the adapter's Root(scope) as the authority rather than the roster's HasPerUserLocation, because the roster is what the manifest layer can check without linking an adapter while the adapter is what knows its own directories
639	- A scope the adapter does not offer is refused rather than resolved to the project root: an asset installed at a scope its author did not ask for lands in a file they have no reason to open, so the refusal is the whole point and the returned root is empty
640	- adapter.UnsupportedScopeError names the asset, its type, the harness and the scope in the {problem, fix} shape, with a remedy that branches on scope — 'remove scope from the entry' is an edit only where a scope was written, so a project-scope refusal directs the author at the entry's targets instead
641	- A zero Scope is treated as project inside ResolveRoot, documented as a restatement rather than a second place the default is decided: an Asset always carries a scope because Interpret is the only route to one, and the guard exists so a zero value cannot produce a diagnostic about a scope nobody wrote
642	- cmd/harnaas/cli/adapter/scope_test.go covers the scope selecting the root (through a test adapter whose two scopes differ, since claudeLike's do not), the undeclared-scope default, the user-scope refusal asserting both the typed diagnostic's four fields and the absence of a project-root fallback, the problem-then-fix shape, the project-scope refusal offering an edit that exists, and task 5.7 asserted as behaviour — an instruction at user scope resolving cleanly here while manifest.ResolveScope refuses it
643	- CLAUDE.md's adapter section records the two load-bearing decisions: why the adapter rather than the roster answers the scope question, and why this layer must not restate a rule the manifest already applied
644	- Tasks 5.5, 5.6 and 5.7 checked off in openspec/changes/add-harnaas-install/tasks.md
645	
646	**Learnings:**
647	- The roster's HasPerUserLocation and an adapter's Root(user) look like the same question and are not: the manifest layer needs an answer it can reach without linking a single adapter, so both checks have to exist, and stating which one wins (the adapter) is what keeps the duplication from becoming a disagreement.
648	- Task 5.7's 'confirm the adapter layer does not re-implement the check' is testable as behaviour rather than only as a comment — resolving an instruction at user scope cleanly through ResolveRoot, in the same test that shows manifest.ResolveScope refusing it, pins both halves so a later change cannot move the rule and leave two places disagreeing.
649	- A diagnostic whose remedy is 'remove the field' is only correct where the field was written. The project-scope branch of UnsupportedScopeError is unreachable from a shipped adapter, but writing one remedy for both scopes would have told an author to delete a `scope` they never wrote — the same class of problem as manifest's nil-versus-empty targets distinction.
650	- claudeLike() gives both scopes the root '.claude', so 'the scope selects the root' is not assertable through it at all — a variant with differing roots is required for the test to mean anything, which is worth noticing before writing an assertion that would pass against a function ignoring its scope argument.
651	- Section 5's remaining tasks all need a write path or an adapter package: 5.8 (containment through a handle anchored at the scope root) and 5.9/5.10 (the tier gate and the unsupported outcome) belong with the install flow, and 5.11's AST boundary test needs at least one adapter package to parse — so 6.5's claude-code adapter is the natural next unit, and ResolveRoot is now the seam it plugs into.

**Changes:**
- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/github is the new kind package: names are resolved with Git and bytes move over HTTPS, because `git ls-remote` goes through the credential helper the user already configured and has no API rate limit, so a private repository resolves without harnaas inventing an auth story
- ResolveRef turns a declared ref into a commit before anything is fetched — a full object identifier is used directly with no remote lookup, an absent ref resolves HEAD, and a name is looked up as the peeled tag, then the tag, then the branch, which is Git's own precedence for a bare name
- Only a full object identifier is taken as one: an abbreviation names whichever object it is unique against today, so one that grew a second match upstream would silently become a different install
- An annotated tag resolves to the commit it peels to rather than to the tag object, which is not what a repository archive is taken from
- Mutability travels with the commit — a branch and the default branch can name something else tomorrow, a tag and a commit identifier cannot — which is what lets the lockfile and lint tell a pin from a moving target
- An unknown ref is detected from the output rather than the exit status, because ls-remote exits successfully having printed nothing; a run that checked the status would report every unknown ref as a resolution to nothing
- The remote's answer is checked for being an object identifier before it can reach a URL, and every ls-remote pattern is built with a `refs/` prefix so a ref out of a manifest can never arrive as something git reads as an option
- runGit sets GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and detaches stdin, closing both routes to a credential prompt that under a CI job or coding agent is not a question anybody answers but the run hanging; git's stderr is folded into the error because an *exec.ExitError reports nothing but a status number
- Three diagnostics: UnknownRefError naming asset, repository and ref; RefLookupError holding the remote raw and redacting where it renders while keeping git's cause unwrappable so a cancelled run stays recognizable; and GitUnavailableError, separate because it is the one ref failure no manifest edit fixes and its message deliberately never names harnaas.json
- Test coverage across an internal file for the seam and an external file for the diagnostics: a full object-identifier table, a commit resolving with a runner that fails the test if called, the refs/-prefix guard driven with an option-shaped ref, peeled-beats-tag and tag-beats-branch, a non-commit answer refused, git missing distinguished from a repository problem, the default-branch path and its argument list, plus real-git tests against a repository built in t.TempDir covering all four ref shapes, an unknown ref and an unreachable remote
- CLAUDE.md gains 'Names are resolved with Git, bytes are moved over HTTPS', recording why resolution is split from retrieval, why only a full identifier skips the lookup, why an unknown ref is a property of the output, and why a missing git is its own diagnostic

**Learnings:**
- `git ls-remote` exits 0 having printed nothing for a ref the remote does not have, so unknown-ref detection can only ever be a property of the output — checking the exit status would report every unknown ref as a resolution to nothing rather than as a failure.
- An explicit `refs/tags/<ref>^{}` pattern is honoured by ls-remote (the peeled entry is printed even when patterns are given), which is what makes annotated-tag resolution one invocation rather than a second peel request. An annotated tag lists its own tag object first and the peeled commit second, so taking the first matching line records the tag object as the commit and fetches an archive that does not exist — proved by reordering the preference, which failed both the stub and the real-git test.
- `git ls-remote <remote> HEAD` answers the default branch's commit directly, and is preferable to `--symref`: the symref form prints two lines whose ref-name column is both times `HEAD`, so a name-to-id map would depend on which line git happened to print last.
- The manifest grammar rejects a `github` source with no `@ref`, so the spec's 'an absent ref resolves the default branch' rule is unreachable from a declared source today — the same situation as the per-user-location refusal in iteration 10. It is implemented and tested directly against the source contract so the first caller that has one does not invent a different answer.
- gosec's G204 fires on any exec with variable arguments even where the executable is a constant; the suppression is only defensible because every pattern is built with a `refs/` prefix, and that property needs its own test (an option-shaped ref asserted to come back prefixed) for the nolint reason to be true rather than merely plausible.
- wrapcheck flags a bare `return nil, err` from `exec.Cmd.Output()` but accepts `fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", err, stderr)`, so folding git's stderr into the error satisfies the linter on the path that has one and only the empty-stderr path needs a wrapper added.
- A package that shells out to git needs testenv's TestMain even though it never asks the standard library for a user directory: git reads the user's global configuration out of $HOME, so a suite run against the real one resolves refs under whatever that machine's owner configured and passes or fails for reasons the test never stated.

### Iteration 21

**Summary:** Implemented the GitHub kind's retrieval half of the add-harnaas-install change — per-run memoized archive fetching keyed by repository and commit, the full Resolve path, and the asset-naming retrieval diagnostic (tasks 3.4–3.5, 15/122 → 17/122) with fmt, lint and the full test suite clean.

**Changes:**
- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/github/archive.go adds the archive endpoint and the per-run memo: the URL is the API's tarball route for a repository at a commit — the commit rather than the ref, so two assets pinned to a tag and to the commit it names are one retrieval — and the memo is a mutex-guarded slot map with a sync.Once per slot, so the lock is never held across a fetch and one repository's retrieval does not queue behind another's
- A retrieval that failed is remembered as well as one that succeeded, because the next asset referencing the same repository would meet the same host and the same answer; the caller attributes the remembered failure to its own asset, so the second asset's diagnostic still names the second asset rather than the first
- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/github/kind.go implements source.Kind end to end: ref to commit, one archive per repository and commit, ExtractSubtree over the subtree the asset names, and NewResolved with provenance recording the requested ref beside the resolved commit and the ref's mutability; New builds it with runGit and source.NewFetcher().Fetch while newKind takes both as parameters so a whole resolution runs with neither git nor a network
- ArchiveRetrievalError names the asset, the repository and the commit — the third being a fact the manifest does not contain — quotes only its cause's problem and keeps the cause unwrappable, so an interrupted run is still recognizable as a cancellation rather than an unreachable repository
- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/problem.go adds source.Problem, which takes a finished diagnostic's problem paragraph and leaves its fix, so a wrapper with a better remedy does not hand the reader two — and carries the transport types' own redaction with it rather than reaching around it
- Test coverage in an internal file for the seam: the archive URL naming the commit and not the ref, a resolution's files and full provenance, a branch resolving mutable, three assets in one repository sharing one fetch, a second commit being its own fetch, eight concurrent resolutions still fetching once, the retrieval diagnostic's three fields, a remembered failure attributed to the asset reading it, and a table over four failure paths each asserting a nil Resolved
- CLAUDE.md records the retrieval decisions — the memo keyed by commit and why the kind is per run, why a failed retrieval is remembered, why the URL is the API tarball endpoint and how that explains the redaction of a signed query — plus the wrapping rule that a diagnostic quotes a cause's problem and never its fix
- golangci.yaml exempts source.ExtractSubtree from wrapcheck, because it is handed the asset, source and commit as its subject precisely so every diagnostic it raises already names them

**Learnings:**
- revive's error-strings rule refuses an errors.New message ending in punctuation, which makes a diagnostic-shaped test fixture (problem, blank line, fix) unspellable as a sentinel — the same constraint iteration 4 met for a package sentinel. A one-line `type diagnostic string` with an Error method is the fixture, and its existence is itself the argument for every harnaas diagnostic being a type rather than a sentinel.
- source.Fetcher.Fetch takes only a URL, so task 3.6's token chain will have to widen that signature or add a headered variant — and the archiveFetcher seam in the github kind will change with it. Choosing api.github.com/repos/<repo>/tarball/<commit> over codeload was what made that a small change rather than a redesign: it is the documented route that takes an authorization header, and it is the redirect-to-a-signed-URL the transport's redirect bound and RedactURL's query-string clause were both written for.
- Memoizing a *failed* retrieval and memoizing a successful one are different decisions with different consequences: the failure has to be stored kind-neutral (the raw transport error) and wrapped per caller, or the second asset's diagnostic names the first asset. Storing the finished ArchiveRetrievalError in the memo would have looked identical in the single-asset test and been wrong in the two-asset one.

Sections 4 and 5 will each wrap the same way.

### Iteration 22

**Summary:** Implemented the GitHub kind's authentication half of the add-harnaas-install change — the token chain, credential-carrying fetch, per-hop credential stripping and the authorization diagnostic (tasks 3.6–3.7, 17/122 → 19/122) with fmt, lint and the full test suite clean.

**Changes:**
- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/credential.go adds source.Credential, which carries the token together with the name of where it was read from, and renders as that origin through String and GoString — so a credential caught by %v, %s, %q or %#v in a message, a log record or a test failure prints the variable rather than the secret, and a diagnostic that must say which token was used has something safe to name
- source.Fetcher.Fetch takes a credential as a parameter rather than gaining a second method, so every fetch answers what it is authenticated as and the unauthenticated request is the zero value rather than a call that forgot to say; the bearer header is set only where a token is present, and a variable holding only whitespace is not present
- The redirect policy drops the authorization header on any hop that leaves the host and port harnaas asked, which is narrower than the rule Go supplies: Go forwards the header across ports of one host, and the hop that matters here is an archive endpoint answering with a signed URL on a content host that carries its own grant — so there is never a hop that both leaves the service and needs the token
- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/github/token.go resolves the chain HARNAAS_GITHUB_TOKEN, GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN in one place and once per run, treating a variable set to nothing as unset because a job that exports a token conditionally leaves an empty value behind and an empty bearer header fails a request that would have succeeded without one; describeTokenChain builds the diagnostic's list from the chain itself rather than restating it
- github.Kind holds the run's credential and passes it into the archive memo, whose key stays repository-and-commit because a run is one identity by construction; the memo still stores the kind-neutral transport failure, so a second asset meeting a remembered refusal gets a message naming itself
- github.AuthorizationError is a distinct diagnostic naming the variable the token came from, or every variable one could have been supplied through when there was none, and deliberately declares no field a token could be put in; its fix is a token rather than a manifest edit, so it never names harnaas.json
- deniesAccess routes 401, 403 and 404 from the archive endpoint to that diagnostic and everything else to ArchiveRetrievalError — 404 included, because ref resolution has already proved over Git that the repository exists and holds the commit, so the forge answering 'not found' is declining to admit to harnaas's HTTP identity what it just admitted to its Git one
- Test coverage: a credential-rendering table over five fmt verbs, a chain table including both empty-value cases, the ambient reader against the process environment, the header presented and absent asserted from the server's side, a proven-non-vacuous redirect-strip test, a sameService port and case table, a six-status table separating a refusal from every other failure, and the authorization diagnostic added to both declared failure lists in errors_test.go
- CLAUDE.md gains 'A token is named by where it came from, never by what it is', recording the chain and its two ambient names, why the credential type renders its origin, why the header is dropped per hop on host and port, and why a 404 is an access decision here

**Learnings:**
- Go's http.Client forwards the Authorization header across a redirect to a different *port* on the same host — its shouldCopyHeaderOnRedirect compares hostnames only. Two httptest servers are both 127.0.0.1, so the strip test fails without harnaas's own per-hop Del, which is what makes it a genuine assertion rather than a restatement of stdlib behaviour. Comparing host plus port (with each scheme's default filled in) is the rule worth holding.
- A 404 from the archive endpoint has to be read as an access decision, not as a missing repository: GitHub answers 404 for a repository the caller may not see, and by the time an archive is fetched ref resolution has already proved over Git — with the user's *Git* credentials, which are not the API token — that the repository exists and holds the commit. Mapping only 401 and 403 would leave the commonest real failure (private repository, no token) reported as a bare status.
- fmt applies a Stringer to %v, %s and %q but not to %#v, which goes to GoString and would otherwise print the struct literal with the token in it. A type holding a secret needs both methods, and the test that proves it needs all the verbs in one rendered string.
- Widening Fetcher.Fetch rather than adding an authenticated variant was the cheaper change and the better rule: the archiveFetcher seam moved with it in one edit, and 'an unauthenticated fetch is the zero Credential' makes forgetting the credential impossible instead of merely discouraged.
- Section 3's remaining tasks are 3.8/3.9 (the content-addressed cache under HARNAAS_CACHE_DIR with a digest check and a bypass) and 3.10 (offline). All three insert at archives.get, which now takes the credential — the cache key is the commit, so the credential stays out of it, but a cached archive fetched under one token being reused under another is a question 3.8 has to answer deliberately.
- perl -pi -e is a safe way to update a repeated Go call site across a test file where sed was not (iteration 21's escape-mangling); the pattern to match on is the argument that is unique to the call, not the function name, when the call spans lines.

### Iteration 23

**Summary:** Implemented the GitHub kind's content-addressed archive cache — location resolution, digest verification before reuse, discard-and-refetch on damage and the caller-facing bypass (tasks 3.8–3.9, 19/122 → 21/122) with fmt, lint and the full test suite clean.

**Changes:**
- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/cache.go adds source.ArchiveCache, the cross-run half of "an archive is fetched at most once": it lives beside the source contract rather than inside the github kind for the reason Fetcher does, and resolves its location from HARNAAS_CACHE_DIR then <user cache dir>/harnaas, with the override naming harnaas's cache root outright so it replaces the default rather than nesting under it
- The store is content-addressed literally — an archive is filed under its own digest and a pointer named by the digest of (kind, repository, commit) records which digest that is — so verifying an entry is comparing the bytes against the name they are filed under, which cannot drift out of step the way a digest recorded beside them could
- Each key field is length-prefixed before hashing, because unframed `acme/assets` at commit `a` and `acme/asset` at commit `sa` serialize identically and one repository would be served the other's content
- A pointer's contents are checked to be a hexadecimal sha256 sum before they are joined into a path, because a file on disk is untrusted input in the same class as an archive entry name; without it a pointer reading `../../elsewhere` is read and then deleted by the discard path
- Nothing in the cache can fail a run: absent, unreadable, pointing at nothing and no-longer-matching-its-digest are one answer, the damaged entry is removed on the way out, and a failed write is a log record rather than an error — and only a fetch that succeeded is filed, which is deliberately the opposite of the in-run memo's rule that a failure is remembered too
- The credential is deliberately not part of the key (the archive of a commit is the same bytes whoever fetched it), with the consequence — an entry is readable by whoever can read its directory — paid for by the default location being the user's own cache directory at 0700/0600
- source.RunOptions carries the run's cache and is handed to every kind at Registry.NewResolver, so the bypass is the absence of a cache rather than a flag on one and a run cannot end up with one kind reading the cache and another not; source.NewKind widened from func() Kind to func(RunOptions) Kind and github.New/newKind/newArchives moved with it
- Test coverage: an internal cache suite over the location seam (reuse across runs, key sensitivity per field, the framing collision, a tampered blob discarded, a pointer to nothing, five refused pointer spellings including a traversal, the bypass, the nowhere-to-live cache) plus a github-level suite proving a second run resolves with the fetcher never called, that the bypass fetches fresh, and that a failed retrieval is not cached
- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/testmain_test.go installs internal/testenv, which the module's AST guardrail requires now that the package asks the standard library for the user's cache directory
- CLAUDE.md gains "A cache entry that cannot prove what it is gets discarded, not returned", recording the store's shape, the framing and hex-check rules, why nothing here can fail a run, why the credential stays out of the key and why the bypass is the absence of a cache

**Learnings:**
- The pointer-contents check is not defensive coding — with it removed, the traversal test failed by having the discard path *delete* the file outside the blob directory that the pointer named. A cache that verifies content but not the name it read the content from can be turned into an arbitrary-file remover by its own cleanup step.
- "Verify an entry against its expected digest" has two shapes, and they are not equivalent: a digest recorded in a sidecar can drift out of step with the bytes beside it, while filing the blob under its own digest makes verification a comparison against the name — which is why the cache is two directories (blobs named by content, pointers named by key) rather than one entry directory holding an archive and a digest file.
- The in-run memo and the cross-run cache take opposite decisions about failure on purpose: the memo remembers a failed retrieval so one outage is not multiplied across the assets that met it, and the cache stores only successes so the outage does not survive the run. Storing a failure in the cache would look identical in every single-run test.
- A cache write must not be able to fail a run, which makes Store an error-free function and its only evidence a log record — the first logging call site in the source package. That is also what settles "which token fetched this" as a non-question: the credential is an access decision, not a content one, so it stays out of the key and the exposure is bounded by the 0700 directory instead.
- Widening source.NewKind to func(RunOptions) Kind is what makes the bypass caller-facing rather than kind-facing: the options are settled once at Registry.NewResolver, so a run cannot hand one kind a cache and forget the next. Task 3.10's offline mode is a second field on the same struct consumed at the same two sites, so it needs no further signature change.
- jsonutil.WriteFileAtomic is the module's atomic writer despite its package name and takes arbitrary bytes, so a tarball goes through it rather than through a second implementation — worth a comment at the call site, since the package name reads as a mismatch.
- Adding a field to an unexported constructor called from ~10 test sites is cheapest with perl -pi -e anchored on the *trailing argument* and end-of-line ($), not on the function name — but the same substitution will silently hit an unrelated append() with a matching tail, so the vet run afterwards is what catches it.

**Summary:** Implemented offline resolution for the GitHub source kind — a network-free run served from the cache, a name refused without any ref lookup, and per-asset diagnostics for both halves (task 3.10, 21/122 → 22/122, completing Section 3) with fmt, lint and the full test suite clean.

**Changes:**
- source.RunOptions gains Offline beside Cache, settled once at Registry.NewResolver so a run is offline for every kind or none; its doc records why failing is the point (skipping, reporting unchanged, or serving whatever commit is cached each turn a run that could not do what it was asked into one that reports success)
- The github archive memo turns a cache miss into a kind-neutral errNotCached instead of a fetch when offline, remembered like any other retrieval failure so a second asset of one repository is not made to wait for the same nothing, and wrapped per caller so each asset's diagnostic names itself
- Ref resolution branches above the lookup rather than inside it: resolveRefOffline resolves a full commit identifier exactly as an online run does and refuses a tag, branch or absent ref outright, so no `git ls-remote` runs at all
- Two diagnostics: OfflineRefError, separate from UnknownRefError because the ref is not known to be wrong, and OfflineArchiveError, separate from ArchiveRetrievalError because nothing was asked so there is no host or status to quote and the remedy is a networked run rather than a manifest edit
- describeRef extracted from RefLookupError into one package function both offline and lookup diagnostics use, so an absent ref is never described two ways
- newKind now takes source.RunOptions rather than a bare cache, so a field added to the run's options reaches the kind without another parameter; ~12 test call sites moved with it
- offline_internal_test.go covers the four spec scenarios: a cached commit resolving with no request of any kind, an uncached commit naming asset/repository/commit, every uncached asset named rather than the first, four ref shapes refused with the runner failing the test if called, offline plus the cache bypass resolving nothing, and an online run still reaching both git and the forge
- CLAUDE.md gains "An offline run refuses a name, and refuses it without asking", and the two new diagnostics are added to both declared failure lists in errors_test.go

**Learnings:**
- The spec's "a branch or tag with no cached resolution" has no producer at the source layer: nothing records ref→commit until section 9's lockfile. The honest implementation is that only a full commit identifier resolves offline — and that costs nothing later, because the lockfile's recorded commit *is* a commit identifier, so task 10.15 is wiring rather than a second offline path.
- The offline branch has to sit above resolveRef rather than inside it. A gitRunner that refused would satisfy "no network request" while violating "no ref lookup is attempted", and would produce the wrong diagnostic — the failure would render as a lookup that failed rather than as one that was never made.
- Vacuity-checking both branches was worth it and only half-confirmed what was expected: disabling the offline archive branch failed three tests, disabling the ref branch failed the four ref-shape cases — but the fully-cached positive test passes either way, because a cache hit and a commit-identifier ref both short-circuit ahead of the offline check. A positive offline test can only ever assert the absence of a request, never the presence of the offline branch.
- An offline miss must be checked before the status classification in retrievalFailure: errNotCached carries no *source.StatusError, so ordering is not load-bearing for correctness today, but a sentinel that reached the ArchiveRetrievalError branch would render "could not retrieve ... : this machine has no cached archive" — a message about a retrieval that never happened.
- Widening newKind from a bare cache to source.RunOptions is what makes the next option free: iteration 23 predicted offline would be "a second field consumed at the same two sites", and that only held for New/Registry — the unexported constructor still needed the widening, so the prediction was right about the design and wrong about the diff.

### Iteration 25

**Summary:** Implemented the `local` source kind of the add-harnaas-install change — reads anchored at `.harnaas`, identical offline resolution, and the missing/escaping/unreadable diagnostics (tasks 4.1–4.2, 22/122 → 24/122) with fmt, lint and the full test suite clean.

**Changes:**
- cmd/harnaas/cli/source/local is the new kind package: it accepts source.RunOptions and deliberately ignores them, because a local read makes no request — so an offline run and a networked one do identical work and the cache has nothing to offer a read costing one syscall, which is the spec's 'local sources still resolve offline' scenario satisfied structurally rather than by a branch
- Every read goes through a handle anchored at `.harnaas` (os.OpenRoot), so containment is the kernel's answer at the moment of the read rather than harnaas's at the moment of the check — the mirror of archive extraction's textual containment, which is textual because an archive already in hand has no filesystem to race with
- Both accepted spellings resolve through one path: the project-local form carries the whole path on the asset, the keyed form splits it between a `local:` sources entry and a path within it, and joining them once leaves every read indifferent to which the author used; a single file resolves under its own leaf name, matching archive extraction's rule
- The walk follows a link only at the asset's own path, where the anchor bounds where it can lead, and refuses one inside the tree as an entry harnaas cannot install — the rule the archive kind already applies, and additionally what makes the walk unable to loop on a link back up the tree
- Five diagnostics in the {problem, fix} shape, each naming the asset and the path relative to the *project root* in the manifest's own spelling: MissingSourceError (a project with no .harnaas at all reports the asset's own path, not the directory), EmptySourceError (a directory somebody created and left empty is not the same mistake as one nobody created), ContainmentError, UnsupportedEntryError and ReadError
- Provenance for a local source records the kind and the source spelled the way the manifest declares it, and claims no ref, commit or mutability — a local source pins nothing, and whether the bytes changed is the digests' question
- Test coverage across an external suite (file and directory shapes, the keyed form, provenance, offline resolving identically to online, missing source, absent .harnaas, empty directory, byte-for-byte content including CRLF and a NUL, the declared-failure-list contract) and an internal suite for the escape classification driven by a real anchored handle
- CLAUDE.md gains 'A local source is read through a handle, and asks nobody anything', recording why the kind ignores the run options, why containment is kernel-enforced here and textual in the archive, why three refusals are told apart, and why the message match is safe

**Learnings:**
- os does not export the sentinel behind a Root's 'path escapes from parent' refusal — os.ErrPathEscapes exists only in the standard library's own export_test.go — so distinguishing an escape from a not-exist and from a permission failure can only be done by matching the message. The fallback is what makes it safe: a rewording reports the containment violation as a read that failed, which is less specific, never wrong, and never lets the read through. Same trade iteration 8 made for encoding/json's unknown-field message.
- os.Symlink fails for an unprivileged Windows user ('A required privilege is not held by the client'), so the two symlink-driven scenarios can only skip on this machine. A `..` component produces the *same* refusal from the same standard-library code with no privilege at all, which is what makes the classification assertable on every platform — worth reaching for even though `..` is unreachable through a manifest, because the grammar strips it long before a read.
- Following symlinks during a directory walk is a loop hazard a visited-set cannot catch: a link back up the tree generates an ever-longer path, so each Stat is a fresh path and only a depth bound or a refusal stops it. Refusing a link inside the selected subtree — which is already the archive kind's rule — removes the hazard without inventing a limit nobody asked for.
- os.Root gained FS() in Go 1.25 returning an fs.FS that implements ReadDirFS/StatFS/ReadFileFS/ReadLinkFS, so `fs.ReadDir(root.FS(), dir)` is the way to enumerate through an anchored handle — Root itself has ReadFile, Stat and Lstat but no ReadDir.
- The local kind is the first source kind to need the project root, and paths.ProjectRoot(ctx) is the sanctioned reader, so it needs no seam of its own: a test passes paths.WithProjectRoot over a t.TempDir. That is cheaper than the parameterized constructors the github kind needed, because there is nothing to stub — no git, no network, no token.
- No size ceiling was added for local reads, deliberately: the spec states ceilings only for archive extraction, and section 8.10 enforces hard limits against *rendered* output. A future iteration wanting one would have to export the per-file and per-asset constants that are currently unexported in package source.
- revive's context-as-argument rule fires on a test helper spelled `func f(tb testing.TB, ctx context.Context, ...)` — the allowed-types-before default covers *testing.T, not testing.TB. Dropping tb from a helper that only needed it for Helper() is cheaper than configuring the linter.

**Learnings:**
- The spec's 'scope root' is the harness's own directory for that scope (<project>/.claude or ~/.claude), not the project root or the home directory — 'Beneath the resolved scope root, map a rule to rules/<id>.md' settles it. That fixes three things at once: Root(scope) is relative and joined by the caller, Destination.Path is relative to the resolved root so it is identical at both scopes, and task 5.8's containment handle anchors at the harness directory rather than at somebody's whole home.
- Making Detect take an fs.FS rather than a directory path turns 'detection has no side effects' into a property of the signature — an fs.FS offers no way to write — and it keeps adapter packages free of os entirely, which will make task 5.11's import allowlist much narrower than it would otherwise have been. os.DirFS implements fs.ReadLinkFS since Go 1.25, so init's deliberate Lstat-not-Stat rule survives the change to fs.
- Registering adapters as values rather than as constructors is the right divergence from source.Registry, and the reason is worth stating in code: source.NewKind exists because a kind memoizes a run's archive fetches, and an adapter has nothing to remember. Copying the constructor form would have implied per-run state and forced every future adapter to have a constructor for no reason.
- A 'no adapter for this harness' lookup failure is not the same class of error as harness.UnknownError from the roster: the roster question is 'does harnaas know this harness' and the registry question is 'can harnaas install a rule for it'. Both are typed and both list alternatives, but conflating them would tell an author to fix a name that is already correct.

### Iteration 28

**Summary:** Implemented adapter-layer scope resolution for the add-harnaas-install change — the adapter's own root per scope, the no-silent-fallback refusal naming asset and harness, and the confirmation that the instruction-at-user-scope rule is not restated (tasks 5.5–5.7, 32/122 → 35/122) with fmt, lint, the full test suite and the e2e suite clean.

- A scope the adapter does not offer is refused rather than resolved to the project root: an asset installed at a scope its author did not ask for lands in a file they have no reason to open, so the refusal is the whole point and the returned root is empty
- adapter.UnsupportedScopeError names the asset, its type, the harness and the scope in the {problem, fix} shape, with a remedy that branches on scope — 'remove scope from the entry' is an edit only where a scope was written, so a project-scope refusal directs the author at the entry's targets instead

**Learnings:**
- The roster's HasPerUserLocation and an adapter's Root(user) look like the same question and are not: the manifest layer needs an answer it can reach without linking a single adapter, so both checks have to exist, and stating which one wins (the adapter) is what keeps the duplication from becoming a disagreement.

- A diagnostic whose remedy is 'remove the field' is only correct where the field was written. The project-scope branch of UnsupportedScopeError is unreachable from a shipped adapter, but writing one remedy for both scopes would have told an author to delete a `scope` they never wrote — the same class of problem as manifest's nil-versus-empty targets distinction.
- claudeLike() gives both scopes the root '.claude', so 'the scope selects the root' is not assertable through it at all — a variant with differing roots is required for the test to mean anything, which is worth noticing before writing an assertion that would pass against a function ignoring its scope argument.

28	
29	- **WHEN** a manifest targets a harness that has no named adapter registered

33

35	named adapter for the target harness. Version 1 SHALL ship exactly one named adapter, `claude-code`.

50

55	harness it is addressing.

58	
59	- **WHEN** the install flow needs the destination for an asset on a named harness
60	- **THEN** it obtains the destination from that harness's adapter with no harness-specific branching
61	
62	#### Scenario: Missing surface is reported, not invented
63	
64	- **WHEN** an adapter has no surface for an asset type

68

70	registry SHALL expose lookup by identity and a listing in a deterministic order independent of
71	registration order. Two adapters registering the same identity is a programming error and MUST fail
72	loudly at startup. A lookup for an unregistered identity SHALL name it and list those registered.
73

83

92	configuration directory existing. Detection MUST create nothing on disk, and MUST report absence
93	rather than an error when the harness is simply not installed.
94	
95	#### Scenario: Present harness is detected
96	
97	- **WHEN** a project contains the Claude Code configuration directory

101

106	
107	Scope SHALL default to `project`, with `user` opt-in. An adapter SHALL offer `user` scope only where
108	that harness's per-user location is unambiguous. Declaring `user` scope for a harness that does not
109	offer it MUST be a validation error naming the harness and the asset, refused before any write, and

113	
114	- **WHEN** an asset declares no scope

118

120	- **THEN** the same relative destination resolves beneath the per-user root instead of the project root
121

123	
124	- **WHEN** an asset declares `user` scope on an adapter with no unambiguous per-user location

132	referenced from `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` or any other file.

135	
136	- **WHEN** a `rule` asset with id `house-style` targets Claude Code at project scope
137	- **THEN** its destination is `house-style.md` in the project's Claude Code rules directory
138

140	
141	- **WHEN** a `persona` asset with id `reviewer` targets Claude Code
142	- **THEN** its destination is `reviewer.md` under the Claude Code agents directory
143	
144	#### Scenario: Rules are never referenced
145	
146	- **WHEN** rule assets are installed for Claude Code
147	- **THEN** no reference to them is added to any memory file or managed block
148

150

152	surface SHALL be written with no note. A `removed` surface MUST be refused with an error naming its

155	install report.

158	
159	- **WHEN** an asset targets a surface whose tier is `removed`

169	- **WHEN** an asset targets a surface whose tier is `legacy`
170	- **THEN** the file is written and the install report carries the deprecation note
171

173	
174	- **WHEN** an asset targets a surface whose tier is `live`
175	- **THEN** the file is written and no tier note is attached to the outcome

178

194

206

211

213	`instruction` asset inlined verbatim, sorted by asset id, each preceded by an HTML comment naming the

218	
219	- **WHEN** instruction assets are installed
220	- **THEN** the block holds each asset's content verbatim, preceded by an HTML comment naming the asset
221	  and the source it came from
222

224	
225	- **WHEN** the manifest's asset order is changed but its instruction set is not
226	- **THEN** the regenerated block is byte-identical, ordered by asset id
227

229	
230	- **WHEN** `AGENTS.md` already contains hand-written content around the markers
231	- **THEN** that content is byte-for-byte unchanged and only the block between the markers is rewritten
232

234	
235	- **WHEN** instruction assets are installed and no `AGENTS.md` exists
236	- **THEN** one is created containing only the managed block
237

239	
240	- **WHEN** the last instruction asset is removed from the manifest and install runs

245	While any instruction asset is installed, harnaas SHALL ensure exactly one `@AGENTS.md` line exists in
246	`CLAUDE.md`, appended at the end of the file, creating `CLAUDE.md` containing only that line when it
247	is absent. When no instruction assets remain, harnaas SHALL remove that line, and MUST delete
248	`CLAUDE.md` only if the file then contains nothing else.
249	
250	#### Scenario: Line is appended to an existing file
251	
252	- **WHEN** instruction assets are installed and `CLAUDE.md` exists without the bridge line
253	- **THEN** the line is appended at the end and the existing content is preserved byte-for-byte
254	
255	#### Scenario: File is created when absent
256	
257	- **WHEN** instruction assets are installed and no `CLAUDE.md` exists
258	- **THEN** `CLAUDE.md` is created containing only the `@AGENTS.md` line
259	
260	#### Scenario: Line is not duplicated
261	
262	- **WHEN** install runs again and the bridge line is already present
263	- **THEN** `CLAUDE.md` is left unchanged and no second line is added
264	
265	#### Scenario: Empty file is deleted on removal
266	
267	- **WHEN** the last instruction asset goes and `CLAUDE.md` contains only the bridge line
268	- **THEN** the line is removed and the file is deleted
269	
270	#### Scenario: File with other content survives removal
271	
272	- **WHEN** the last instruction asset goes and `CLAUDE.md` contains other content
273	- **THEN** only the bridge line is removed and the file is kept
274	
275	### Requirement: Adapter Import Boundary
276	
277	Adapter packages SHALL import only the adapter contract package and general-purpose utilities, and
278	MUST NOT import the install, lockfile or command-layer packages. A hand-written test SHALL parse each
279	adapter package's syntax tree and fail on any import outside an explicit allowlist. That same test
280	MUST assert every adapter package registers itself, so no adapter is silently missing from the
281	registry.
282	
283	#### Scenario: Forbidden import fails the test
284	
285	- **WHEN** an adapter package imports the install flow
286	- **THEN** the boundary test fails naming the offending package and import
287	
288	#### Scenario: Widening the boundary is deliberate
289	
290	- **WHEN** an adapter needs a package outside the current allowlist
291	- **THEN** the test fails until the allowlist is edited explicitly to admit it
292	
293	#### Scenario: Missing self-registration fails the test
294	
295	- **WHEN** an adapter package exists but does not register itself
296	- **THEN** the same test fails naming that package

2	//
3	// Most harnesses need no adapter at all. Of the harnesses surveyed for this
4	// design, 17 read `.agents/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` and 21 read `AGENTS.md`, so a
5	// skill and an instruction reach them through shared locations that no
6	// per-harness code computes. What has no shared equivalent anywhere is a rule, a
7	// command and a persona, and those reach a harness only through an adapter that
8	// knows its directories. Version 1 ships exactly one, `claude-code`, and "a
9	// harness with no adapter" is a supported state rather than a gap.
10	//
11	// This package is the contract and the registry; each adapter is its own package
12	// beneath it. The split is the extraction rule doing its work rather than a layer
13	// for its own sake: the install flow lives in the flat cli package and has to
14	// import the adapters, so an adapter importing a contract that lived beside the
15	// flow would be an import cycle one file later. Keeping the contract here is also
16	// what makes the import boundary checkable — an adapter may reach this package
17	// and general-purpose utilities, and nothing else.
18	//
19	// An adapter answers questions and performs no I/O of its own. It is handed a
20	// filesystem to detect through and it returns paths for the caller to write, for
21	// the same reason the harness roster holds no behaviour: two things that can each
22	// compute a destination eventually compute two different ones.
23	package adapter
24	
25	import (
26		"io/fs"
27	
28		"github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/harness"
29		"github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/manifest"
30	)
31	
32	// Adapter maps assets onto the files one harness reads.
33	//
34	// The contract is uniform on purpose: the install flow obtains a destination
35	// without knowing which harness it is addressing, so adding the second adapter
36	// is additive rather than another branch in the flow.
37	type Adapter interface {
38		// Harness is the identity this adapter registers under, and the exact
39		// string a manifest writes in `harnesses` or in an asset's `targets`.
40		Harness() harness.ID
41	
42		// Detect reports whether the project already shows evidence of this
43		// harness — its configuration directory existing, or a file only it
44		// writes.
45		//
46		// The parameter is a filesystem rather than a directory path because
47		// detection must create nothing: an fs.FS offers no way to write, so
48		// "detection has no side effects" is a property of the signature rather
49		// than a rule each adapter has to honour. A harness that is simply not
50		// installed is an absence and never a failure — there is nothing for a
51		// caller to do about it and nothing to report.
52		Detect(project fs.FS) bool
53	
54		// Root returns the harness's own directory for one scope, relative to that
55		// scope's root: the project root at `project` scope, and the user's home
56		// directory at `user` scope. The second result is false where the harness
57		// has no unambiguous location for that scope, which is the whole of the
58		// adapter's answer to whether an asset may declare it.
59		//
60		// It is relative, and joined by the caller, because an adapter that read
61		// the environment for a home directory would be a second place in harnaas
62		// deciding where a user's files live.
63		Root(scope manifest.Scope) (string, bool)
64	
65		// Destination returns where one asset installs on this harness, relative to
66		// the resolved scope root — the harness's own directory for the asset's
67		// scope, which is [Adapter.Root] joined to the project root or to the
68		// user's home. A rule resolves to `rules/house-style.md` there, never to a
69		// path counted from the project root, so the same mapping serves both
70		// scopes and the lockfile can record a destination that means the same
71		// thing on another machine.
72		//
73		// The second result is false where this harness has no surface for the
74		// asset's type. That absence is a value rather than an invented path
75		// precisely because a guessed destination is indistinguishable from a real
76		// one once it is written: the caller reports the pairing as unsupported and
77		// installs the asset's other targets.
78		//
79		// The asset travels whole rather than as the type, id and scope a mapping
80		// reads, for the reason a source request does: the fields a diagnostic needs
81		// are not the fields the mapping needs, and narrowing the parameter would
82		// make every caller's messages worse to keep a signature shorter.
83		Destination(asset manifest.Asset) (Destination, bool)
84	}
85	
86	// Destination is where one asset installs on one harness, together with the
87	// terms it installs on.
88	//
89	// The terms travel with the path because they are decided by the same lookup:
90	// which surface a type maps to is what settles how current that surface is and
91	// what has to happen to the bytes on their way into it. Splitting them would let
92	// a caller obtain a path and write it without ever asking whether the harness
93	// still reads there.
94	type Destination struct {
95		// Path is the installed file relative to the resolved scope root,
96		// slash-separated. Whether it stays inside that root is not this value's
97		// promise: the write goes through a handle anchored there, so an asset id
98		// that would escape is refused by the kernel at the moment of the write
99		// rather than by a comparison at the moment it was computed.
100		Path string
101	
102		// Tier is how current the surface is, which decides whether harnaas writes
103		// here at all.
104		Tier Tier
105	
106		// Replacement names the surface that superseded a removed one, and is set
107		// only where Tier is [TierRemoved]. It is what makes the refusal actionable:
108		// the reader is being told the harness stopped reading this path, and the
109		// only useful next sentence is where it reads instead.
110		Replacement string
111	
112		// Note is the sentence the install report carries for a gated or a legacy
113		// surface — the setup the user still has to perform, or the deprecation
114		// they should plan for. A live surface carries none, because a note nobody
115		// has to act on teaches a reader to skip them all.
116		Note string
117	
118		// Renderer names the transformation from the source's bytes to the ones
119		// that land here. It is a name rather than a function because an adapter
120		// declares what a surface needs while the rendering layer owns how it is
121		// done: an adapter carrying an implementation would import the layer the
122		// import boundary exists to keep out.
123		Renderer Renderer
124	}
125	
126	// Tier is how current a harness surface is, which decides whether harnaas writes
127	// to it.
128	//
129	// It exists because a harness that has moved on from a path does not say so: the
130	// write succeeds, the file appears, and nothing ever reads it. That is the exact
131	// outcome a tool whose purpose is telling a team what is in effect must not
132	// produce, so the state of a surface is data harnaas carries rather than
133	// something a user discovers.
134	type Tier string
135	
136	const (
137		// TierLive is a surface the harness reads today. It is written with no
138		// note, which is what keeps the notes on the other tiers worth reading.
139		TierLive Tier = "live"
140	
141		// TierGated is a surface the harness reads only once the user has enabled
142		// something. It is written, with the setup note carried into the install
143		// report, because the file is correct and the remaining step is theirs.
144		TierGated Tier = "gated"
145	
146		// TierLegacy is a surface the harness still reads but has deprecated. It is
147		// written, with the deprecation note carried into the report, so a team
148		// learns before the surface becomes removed rather than after.
149		TierLegacy Tier = "legacy"
150	
151		// TierRemoved is a surface the harness no longer reads. Writing there is a
152		// guaranteed silent no-op, so it is refused rather than written, naming the
153		// surface that replaced it.
154		TierRemoved Tier = "removed"
155	)
156	
157	// Renderer names the transformation between a source's bytes and the bytes that
158	// land at a destination.
159	//
160	// A name rather than a function keeps the adapter layer and the rendering layer
161	// apart, and it is also what makes a surface able to declare a renderer nobody
162	// has written yet: selecting one with no implementation reports the pairing
163	// unsupported and names the renderer, which is a truthful outcome, where falling
164	// back to copying the bytes would write a file the harness cannot read.
165	type Renderer string
166	
167	const (
168		// RendererIdentity reproduces the source bytes exactly, including
169		// frontmatter, line endings and trailing whitespace. It is what almost
170		// every surface declares, and it is deliberately a renderer rather than the
171		// absence of one: copying is the default, not the rule.
172		RendererIdentity Renderer = "identity"
173	
174		// RendererAsSkill delivers an asset through a harness's skill surface when
175		// its own surface is absent — a command as a SKILL.md the model is told not
176		// to invoke on its own initiative. It is an emulation, and is reported as
177		// one rather than as plain success.
178		RendererAsSkill Renderer = "as-skill"
179	)
