2	
3	import (
4		"fmt"
5		"slices"
6		"strings"
7		"sync"
8	
9		"github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/harness"
10		"github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/manifest"
11	)
12	
13	// Registry is the set of named adapters this binary can install through, keyed
14	// by the harness each one addresses.
15	//
16	// A registry value rather than one package-level map is what lets a test
17	// exercise lookup — including the failure for a harness nobody wrote an adapter
18	// for — without reaching into the set the binary itself ships.
19	type Registry struct {
20		mu sync.Mutex
21	
22		// adapters holds each adapter as a value rather than a constructor, which is
23		// deliberately unlike the source-kind registry: a kind remembers which
24		// archives this run has already fetched and so belongs to the run, while an
25		// adapter is a mapping from an asset to a path and has nothing to remember.
26		// Handing every run its own copy of a pure mapping would suggest it did.
27		adapters map[harness.ID]Adapter
28	}
29	
30	// Default is the registry the adapters shipped with this binary register into,
31	// and the one the install flow resolves destinations through. An adapter package
32	// registers itself from its own init, so an adapter that has been linked in is an
33	// adapter that works.
34	var Default = &Registry{}
35	
36	// Register adds an adapter to [Default].
37	func Register(adapter Adapter) {
38		Default.Register(adapter)
39	}
40	
41	// Register adds an adapter under the harness it addresses.
42	//
43	// A second adapter for one harness panics rather than replacing or ignoring the
44	// first. Registration happens during package initialization, before the process
45	// has read anything, so the only way to reach it is a mistake in harnaas's own
46	// wiring — and both silent outcomes are a binary that installs through whichever
47	// adapter happened to be linked last.
48	func (r *Registry) Register(adapter Adapter) {
49		id := adapter.Harness()
50	
51		r.mu.Lock()
52		defer r.mu.Unlock()
53	
54		if r.adapters == nil {
55			r.adapters = make(map[harness.ID]Adapter)
56		}
57		if _, registered := r.adapters[id]; registered {
58			panic(fmt.Sprintf("adapter: harness %q has two adapters registered", id))
59		}
60		r.adapters[id] = adapter
61	}
62	
63	// Lookup returns the adapter for a harness.
64	//
65	// A harness with no adapter is not a broken install by itself: skills and
66	// instructions reach every harness through shared locations, and this lookup only
67	// happens for the types that have no shared equivalent. That is why the failure
68	// is a typed diagnostic the caller can attribute to the asset that needed it,
69	// rather than something the registry decides is fatal.
70	func (r *Registry) Lookup(id harness.ID) (Adapter, error) {
71		r.mu.Lock()
72		defer r.mu.Unlock()
73	
74		adapter, registered := r.adapters[id]
75		if !registered {
76			return nil, &NotRegisteredError{Harness: id, Registered: r.harnessesLocked()}
77		}
78		return adapter, nil
79	}
80	
81	// Registered reports whether a harness has a named adapter.
82	//
83	// It is separate from [Registry.Lookup] because the install flow asks the
84	// question long before it has an asset to blame for the answer: a harness with no
85	// adapter still installs every shared asset, and building a diagnostic to throw
86	// away would be the wrong shape for that path.
87	func (r *Registry) Registered(id harness.ID) bool {
88		r.mu.Lock()
89		defer r.mu.Unlock()
90	
91		_, registered := r.adapters[id]
92		return registered
93	}
94	
95	// Harnesses returns every harness with a named adapter, sorted.
96	//
97	// Sorted rather than in registration order, because registration order is
98	// whatever the import graph happens to produce and this list is rendered into the
99	// message a user reads when their harness is not among them.
100	func (r *Registry) Harnesses() []harness.ID {
101		r.mu.Lock()
102		defer r.mu.Unlock()
103	
104		return r.harnessesLocked()
105	}
106	
107	// Adapters returns every registered adapter, in [Registry.Harnesses] order, so a
108	// caller that walks them reports the same thing on every run.
109	func (r *Registry) Adapters() []Adapter {
110		r.mu.Lock()
111		defer r.mu.Unlock()
112	
113		adapters := make([]Adapter, 0, len(r.adapters))
114		for _, id := range r.harnessesLocked() {
115			adapters = append(adapters, r.adapters[id])
116		}
117		return adapters
118	}
119	
120	// harnessesLocked returns the registered harnesses in sorted order. The caller
121	// holds the lock.
122	func (r *Registry) harnessesLocked() []harness.ID {
123		ids := make([]harness.ID, 0, len(r.adapters))
124		for id := range r.adapters {
125			ids = append(ids, id)
126		}
127		slices.Sort(ids)
128		return ids
129	}
130	
131	// NotRegisteredError reports a harness this binary has no named adapter for.
132	//
133	// The manifest layer has already accepted the name, because the roster
134	// recognizes more harnesses than there are adapters and that is the intended
135	// state: a harness harnaas knows about receives every shared asset without one.
136	// So the problem is never "this harness does not exist" — it is that the asset in
137	// hand is of a type with no shared equivalent, and the message has to say which
138	// harnesses could have taken it.
139	type NotRegisteredError struct {
140		// Harness is the harness with no adapter, exactly as the manifest wrote it.
141		Harness harness.ID
142	
143		// Registered is every harness this binary has an adapter for, sorted.
144		Registered []harness.ID
145	}
146	
147	// Error states the problem and then the fix, as every user-facing diagnostic
148	// does.
149	func (e *NotRegisteredError) Error() string {
150		return fmt.Sprintf(
151			"harnaas has no adapter for the harness %q, and a %s, %s or %s asset has no shared location to install to\n\n"+
152				"%s Skills and instructions need no adapter and install for every harness harnaas recognizes.",
153			e.Harness,
154			manifest.AssetTypeRule, manifest.AssetTypeCommand, manifest.AssetTypePersona,
155			e.remedy(),
156		)
157	}
158	
159	// remedy names the harnesses that would have worked, or says plainly that there
160	// are none. An empty registry is unreachable from a built binary — it links at
161	// least one adapter — but a message reading "target one of: ." is worse than one
162	// stating the situation.
163	func (e *NotRegisteredError) remedy() string {
164		if len(e.Registered) == 0 {
165			return fmt.Sprintf("This harnaas has no adapters at all, so remove the entry from %s.", manifest.FileName)
166		}
167	
168		names := make([]string, 0, len(e.Registered))
169		for _, id := range e.Registered {
170			names = append(names, fmt.Sprintf("%q", id))
171		}
172	
173		return fmt.Sprintf(
174			"Change the entry's %q in %s to a harness harnaas has an adapter for: %s.",
175			"targets", manifest.FileName, strings.Join(names, ", "),
176		)
177	}

## Decisions

### Shared targets first; a named adapter is the exception

Recorded in
[0002-shared-agents-target-before-per-harness.md](../../../docs/adr/0002-shared-agents-target-before-per-harness.md).
Its consequence for this change is structural: support is two-tiered. `skill` and `instruction` reach
a harness through shared locations with no per-harness code, while `rule`, `command` and `persona` —
which have no shared equivalent anywhere — reach it only through a named adapter. v1 ships exactly one
named adapter and still serves most of the ecosystem, and "harness with no adapter" is a supported
state rather than a gap.

This is also why the `harnesses` list in the manifest means "the harnesses we guarantee", not "the
harnesses that will see this". A shared directory is visible to every harness installed on the
machine. Nothing in the design can change that, so the lockfile records which harness an adapter
resolved a destination *for*, as attribution rather than exclusive ownership.

### Ownership lives in the lockfile

Recorded in
[0001-ownership-lives-in-the-lockfile.md](../../../docs/adr/0001-ownership-lives-in-the-lockfile.md).
Two consequences are specified rather than left implicit, because both look like bugs if you meet
them without the rule: deleting the lockfile does not orphan installed files, it makes them
unmanaged, which is protective; and a project with pre-existing harness files gets conflict reports on
its first install rather than a silent takeover.

The shared-target decision sharpens this. Ownership in `.agents/` is a seventeen-way problem, and
other tools write there too. The lockfile rule is what makes that safe without negotiation: another
tool's file at a destination `harnaas` wants is simply an unmanaged conflict — reported, never
overwritten.

### Force applies to drift, never to unmanaged files

`--force` overwrites a managed destination whose content no longer matches what was recorded. It
deliberately does not override unmanaged-path protection. The two situations look similar and are
not. A drifted managed file is something `harnaas` put there and the user edited, so restoring it is
recoverable and comprehensible. An unmanaged file was never `harnaas`'s, and no flag on an install
command should be able to destroy it. A user who wants `harnaas` to own that path deletes it
themselves, which is an explicit act with an obvious meaning.

### Rendering is the general case; verbatim copying is only the default

This is the decision that most changed shape during design, and it sits in apparent tension with ADR
0001, which rejected in-file markers partly because injecting one would mean the installed bytes never
equal the source bytes.

The resolution is that byte-equality with upstream was never the invariant worth defending. The
question that matters is *"does this destination still hold what `harnaas` wrote?"*, and that is
answered by comparing the destination against a recorded **installed digest**. A separate **source
digest** answers *"has upstream moved?"*. Once those two comparisons are independent, a transformation
between source and destination stops being a threat to drift detection, and copying verbatim becomes
merely the renderer that happens to apply almost everywhere.

Markers remain wrong for the reasons the ADR gives that this does not touch: a comment is not valid
syntax in every format, ownership expressed in file content evaporates when someone edits the file,
and a marker cannot express "this directory of twelve files is mine". Ownership stays in the lockfile;
the bytes are free.

The payoff is that `as-skill` — delivering a `command` to a harness with no command surface, as a
`SKILL.md` with model invocation disabled — is expressible at all, and that adding a format converter
later needs no redesign. The render hook is therefore part of the adapter contract in v1 even though
only two renderers exist, because widening an interface after adapters exist is the expensive move.

### Refuse rather than produce a silent no-op

One principle explains five requirements that otherwise look unrelated and unusually strict:

- a `removed` support tier is refused rather than written, because the harness ignores that path;
- a skill whose frontmatter `name` disagrees with its inferred id fails resolution, because several
  harnesses drop it without a message;
- the 1 MB `SKILL.md`, 4 MiB memory file and depth-5 import limits fail the asset, because a file past
  them is skipped by the harness;
- a declared-but-unimplemented renderer reports `unsupported` and never falls back to identity,
  because identity would write a file the harness cannot read;
- a `rule` declaring `paths:` is `unsupported` on a harness with no rules directory rather than
  emulated as an instruction, because emulation would silently widen it from scoped to always-on.

In every case the alternative is a green install and a harness that quietly ignores the file — the
single worst outcome for a tool whose whole purpose is telling a team what is actually in effect. The
40,000-character assembled-content threshold is deliberately *not* in this list: it is a degradation

answered by comparing the destination against a recorded **installed digest**. A separate **source
digest** answers *"has upstream moved?"*. Once those two comparisons are independent, a transformation
between source and destination stops being a threat to drift detection, and copying verbatim becomes
merely the renderer that happens to apply almost everywhere.

Markers remain wrong for the reasons the ADR gives that this does not touch: a comment is not valid
syntax in every format, ownership expressed in file content evaporates when someone edits the file,
and a marker cannot express "this directory of twelve files is mine". Ownership stays in the lockfile;
the bytes are free.

The payoff is that `as-skill` — delivering a `command` to a harness with no command surface, as a
`SKILL.md` with model invocation disabled — is expressible at all, and that adding a format converter
later needs no redesign. The render hook is therefore part of the adapter contract in v1 even though
only two renderers exist, because widening an interface after adapters exist is the expensive move.

### Refuse rather than produce a silent no-op

One principle explains five requirements that otherwise look unrelated and unusually strict:

- a `removed` support tier is refused rather than written, because the harness ignores that path;
- a skill whose frontmatter `name` disagrees with its inferred id fails resolution, because several
  harnesses drop it without a message;
- the 1 MB `SKILL.md`, 4 MiB memory file and depth-5 import limits fail the asset, because a file past
  them is skipped by the harness;
- a declared-but-unimplemented renderer reports `unsupported` and never falls back to identity,
  because identity would write a file the harness cannot read;
- a `rule` declaring `paths:` is `unsupported` on a harness with no rules directory rather than
  emulated as an instruction, because emulation would silently widen it from scoped to always-on.

In every case the alternative is a green install and a harness that quietly ignores the file — the
single worst outcome for a tool whose whole purpose is telling a team what is actually in effect. The
40,000-character assembled-content threshold is deliberately *not* in this list: it is a degradation

# Skills install to the shared `.agents/` directory before a harness's own

A survey of 23 AI coding harnesses found that 17 of them read `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, and
21 read `AGENTS.md`. harnaas therefore writes skills to the shared location first and falls back to a
harness's own directory only where that harness does not read the shared one. The obvious design —
one directory tree per harness — is deliberately not what we do.

## Considered Options

Per-harness directories (`.claude/skills/`, `.cursor/skills/`, …) are more explicit: declaring a
harness would mean something concrete, and ownership would be unambiguous. They were rejected because
they produce N byte-identical copies of every skill, N lockfile installations, and N things to keep in
step — to buy explicitness the ecosystem has already stopped needing.

## Consequences

Two costs are accepted deliberately.

A shared directory is visible to **every** installed harness, not only the ones listed in
`harnaas.json`. The `harnesses` list therefore means "which harnesses we guarantee", not "which
harnesses will see this".

Ownership in the shared directory is a 17-way problem rather than a 2-way one, and other tools write
there too — `openspec` among them. The lockfile rule in
[0001](./0001-ownership-lives-in-the-lockfile.md) is what makes this safe: another tool's file at a
destination harnaas wants is simply an unmanaged conflict, reported and never overwritten.

1	package adapter
2	
3	import (
4		"fmt"
5	
6		"github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/harness"
7		"github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/manifest"
8	)
9	
10	// ResolveRoot returns the harness directory an asset installs beneath: the
11	// adapter's own root for the asset's scope, relative to that scope's own root —
12	// the project root at `project` scope, the user's home at `user` scope.
13	//
14	// Which scope an asset has is settled long before this: [manifest.Interpret]
15	// defaults an undeclared one to `project`, refuses a scope harnaas does not
16	// define, and refuses `user` where the *roster* records no per-user location.
17	// What is left for this layer is the question only an adapter can answer — does
18	// this harness have an unambiguous location for that scope — and the roster's
19	// answer is deliberately not taken as this one. The roster is a fact about a
20	// harness the manifest layer can check without linking a single adapter; the
21	// adapter is the thing that actually knows its own directories, and where the
22	// two disagree the adapter is right.
23	//
24	// A refusal is a refusal, never a quieter install: an asset that asked for
25	// `user` scope and was given the project root would be installed somewhere its
26	// author did not ask for, in a file they would have no reason to look at.
27	func ResolveRoot(a Adapter, asset manifest.Asset) (string, error) {
28		scope := asset.Scope
29		if scope == "" {
30			// An Asset always carries a scope, because Interpret is the only route
31			// to one and it defaults an undeclared field. The restatement is not a
32			// second place the default is decided — it is what stops a zero value
33			// reaching a.Root("") and producing a diagnostic about a scope nobody
34			// wrote.
35			scope = manifest.ScopeProject
36		}
37	
38		root, offered := a.Root(scope)
39		if !offered {
40			return "", &UnsupportedScopeError{
41				AssetID: asset.ID,
42				Type:    asset.Type,
43				Harness: a.Harness(),
44				Scope:   scope,
45			}
46		}
47	
48		return root, nil
49	}
50	
51	// UnsupportedScopeError reports an asset whose scope this harness has no
52	// unambiguous directory for.
53	//
54	// It names the asset and the harness because the pairing is what is wrong:
55	// `user` scope is correct for the asset and the harness is correct for the
56	// project, and only together do they name a location harnaas would have to
57	// invent. Inventing one is the outcome this refusal exists to prevent — an
58	// asset installed under a guessed per-user directory reports success, is never
59	// read, and leaves the team believing it is in effect.
60	type UnsupportedScopeError struct {
61		// AssetID is the asset that asked for the scope.
62		AssetID string
63	
64		// Type is the asset's type, which is how the message names it in the
65		// author's own vocabulary rather than as "the asset".
66		Type manifest.AssetType
67	
68		// Harness is the harness with no directory for that scope.
69		Harness harness.ID
70	
71		// Scope is the scope that could not be resolved.
72		Scope manifest.Scope
73	}
74	
75	// Error states the problem and then the fix, as every user-facing diagnostic
76	// does.
77	func (e *UnsupportedScopeError) Error() string {
78		return fmt.Sprintf(
79			"the %s %q installs at %q scope, and the harness %q has no unambiguous location for that scope\n\n"+
80				"%s",
81			e.Type, e.AssetID, e.Scope, e.Harness,
82			e.remedy(),
83		)
84	}
85	
86	// remedy names the edit that fixes it, which depends on which scope was asked
87	// for. Dropping the scope is an edit only where there is a scope to drop: at
88	// `project` scope there is nothing to remove and the entry's only route to a
89	// harness that can take it is its `targets`.
90	func (e *UnsupportedScopeError) remedy() string {
91		if e.Scope == manifest.ScopeUser {
92			return fmt.Sprintf(
93				"Remove %q from the entry in %s so it installs at %q scope, or narrow the entry's %q to harnesses with a per-user location.",
94				"scope", manifest.FileName, manifest.ScopeProject, "targets",
95			)
96		}
97	
98		return fmt.Sprintf(
99			"Remove %q from the entry's %q in %s.",
100			e.Harness, "targets", manifest.FileName,
101		)
102	}
103

1	package adapter_test
2	
3	import (
4		"io/fs"
5		"path"
6		"testing"
7		"testing/fstest"
8	
9		"github.com/stretchr/testify/assert"
10	
11		"github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/adapter"
12		"github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/harness"
13		"github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/manifest"
14	)
15	
16	// testAdapter is an adapter shaped like the ones harnaas will ship: a directory
17	// per scope, a surface for some types and none for others.
18	//
19	// The contract is what these tests are about, so the surfaces are declared as
20	// data rather than mapped by a method — an adapter that computed them would be
21	// asserting its own arithmetic instead of the shape every adapter has to present.
22	type testAdapter struct {
23		id harness.ID
24	
25		// roots is the harness's directory per scope. A scope absent from the map is
26		// one this adapter does not offer.
27		roots map[manifest.Scope]string
28	
29		// surfaces is the destination for each asset type this harness has one for,
30		// relative to the scope root, with `{id}` standing in for the asset id.
31		surfaces map[manifest.AssetType]adapter.Destination
32	
33		// evidence is the path whose presence means the harness is in use.
34		evidence string
35	}
36	
37	var _ adapter.Adapter = (*testAdapter)(nil)
38	
39	func (a *testAdapter) Harness() harness.ID { return a.id }
40	
41	func (a *testAdapter) Detect(project fs.FS) bool {
42		_, err := fs.Stat(project, a.evidence)
43		return err == nil
44	}
45	
46	func (a *testAdapter) Root(scope manifest.Scope) (string, bool) {
47		root, offered := a.roots[scope]
48		return root, offered
49	}
50	
51	func (a *testAdapter) Destination(asset manifest.Asset) (adapter.Destination, bool) {
52		surface, supported := a.surfaces[asset.Type]
53		if !supported {
54			return adapter.Destination{}, false
55		}
56		if _, offered := a.roots[asset.Scope]; !offered {
57			return adapter.Destination{}, false
58		}
59	
60		surface.Path = path.Join(surface.Path, asset.ID+".md")
61		return surface, true
62	}
63	
64	// claudeLike is the adapter these tests exercise the contract through: two
65	// scopes, a live rules surface, and no surface at all for a persona.
66	func claudeLike() *testAdapter {
67		return &testAdapter{
68			id: harness.ClaudeCode,
69			roots: map[manifest.Scope]string{
70				manifest.ScopeProject: ".claude",
71				manifest.ScopeUser:    ".claude",
72			},
73			surfaces: map[manifest.AssetType]adapter.Destination{
74				manifest.AssetTypeRule: {Path: "rules", Tier: adapter.TierLive, Renderer: adapter.RendererIdentity},
75			},
76			evidence: ".claude",
77		}
78	}
79	
80	func asset(assetType manifest.AssetType, id string, scope manifest.Scope) manifest.Asset {
81		return manifest.Asset{Type: assetType, ID: id, Targets: []harness.ID{harness.ClaudeCode}, Scope: scope}
82	}
83	
84	// TestDestinationIsRelativeToTheResolvedScopeRoot pins the one thing every
85	// caller of the contract depends on: the same mapping serves both scopes, so the
86	// path the lockfile records means the same thing on another machine.
87	func TestDestinationIsRelativeToTheResolvedScopeRoot(t *testing.T) {
88		t.Parallel()
89	
90		a := claudeLike()
91	
92		project, found := a.Destination(asset(manifest.AssetTypeRule, "house-style", manifest.ScopeProject))
93		assert.True(t, found)
94		assert.Equal(t, "rules/house-style.md", project.Path)
95	
96		user, found := a.Destination(asset(manifest.AssetTypeRule, "house-style", manifest.ScopeUser))
97		assert.True(t, found)
98		assert.Equal(t, project.Path, user.Path, "the scope moves the root, not the destination beneath it")
99	}
100	
101	// TestNoSurfaceForATypeIsReportedRatherThanInvented is task 5.2's whole point.
102	// A guessed path is indistinguishable from a real one once it has been written,
103	// so the absence has to be a value the caller cannot mistake for a destination.
104	func TestNoSurfaceForATypeIsReportedRatherThanInvented(t *testing.T) {
105		t.Parallel()
106	
107		destination, found := claudeLike().Destination(asset(manifest.AssetTypePersona, "reviewer", manifest.ScopeProject))
108	
109		assert.False(t, found)
110		assert.Equal(t, adapter.Destination{}, destination, "nothing a caller could write is handed back")
111	}
112	
113	// TestAScopeTheAdapterDoesNotOfferHasNoRootAndNoDestination is the shape scope
114	// validation reads: an adapter states the scopes it has an unambiguous location
115	// for, and states it in one place.
116	func TestAScopeTheAdapterDoesNotOfferHasNoRootAndNoDestination(t *testing.T) {
117		t.Parallel()
118	
119		projectOnly := claudeLike()
120		delete(projectOnly.roots, manifest.ScopeUser)
121	
122		root, offered := projectOnly.Root(manifest.ScopeUser)
123		assert.False(t, offered)
124		assert.Empty(t, root)
125	
126		destination, found := projectOnly.Destination(asset(manifest.AssetTypeRule, "house-style", manifest.ScopeUser))
127		assert.False(t, found)
128		assert.Equal(t, adapter.Destination{}, destination)
129	}
130	
131	func TestRootIsRelativeToTheScopesOwnRoot(t *testing.T) {
132		t.Parallel()
133	
134		for _, scope := range []manifest.Scope{manifest.ScopeProject, manifest.ScopeUser} {
135			root, offered := claudeLike().Root(scope)
136	
137			assert.True(t, offered)
138			assert.Equal(t, ".claude", root)
139			assert.False(t, path.IsAbs(root), "an adapter never decides where a user's files live")
140		}
141	}
142	
143	// TestDetectionReadsAndCreatesNothing is carried by the signature rather than by
144	// this test — an fs.FS has no way to write — so what is asserted here is the
145	// other half: a harness that is simply not installed is an absence, never a
146	// failure a caller has to handle.
147	func TestDetectionReadsAndCreatesNothing(t *testing.T) {
148		t.Parallel()
149	
150		using := fstest.MapFS{".claude/settings.json": &fstest.MapFile{}}
151		assert.True(t, claudeLike().Detect(using))
152	
153		empty := fstest.MapFS{"README.md": &fstest.MapFile{}}
154		assert.False(t, claudeLike().Detect(empty))
155	}
156	
157	// TestASurfaceCarriesItsTermsWithItsPath is why [adapter.Destination] is one
158	// value: a caller cannot obtain a path and write it without having been told
159	// whether the harness still reads there and what has to happen to the bytes.
160	func TestASurfaceCarriesItsTermsWithItsPath(t *testing.T) {
161		t.Parallel()
162	
163		removed := claudeLike()
164		removed.surfaces[manifest.AssetTypeCommand] = adapter.Destination{
165			Path:        "commands",
166			Tier:        adapter.TierRemoved,
167			Replacement: ".claude/skills",
168		}
169	
170		destination, found := removed.Destination(asset(manifest.AssetTypeCommand, "review", manifest.ScopeProject))
171	
172		assert.True(t, found)
173		assert.Equal(t, "commands/review.md", destination.Path)
174		assert.Equal(t, adapter.TierRemoved, destination.Tier)
175		assert.Equal(t, ".claude/skills", destination.Replacement)
176	}

### The one adapter maps three types, and says nothing about the other two

`cmd/harnaas/cli/adapter/claudecode` is v1's only named adapter: `.claude` at both scopes, a rule at
`rules/<id>.md`, a command at `commands/<id>.md` and a persona at `agents/<id>.md`, each with the
asset id as the stem. A `skill` and an `instruction` are deliberately *absent* from that table rather
than mapped into `.claude` as well — they reach every harness through shared locations, and an
adapter answering for them would be a second place harnaas decides where a skill lands. The scope
does not enter the mapping at all: it selects the root the path is joined beneath, which is
`Root`'s answer asked once by `ResolveRoot`, so one relative path serves both scopes.

Detection reads the *roster's* evidence rather than a second list, because `init` detecting a harness
to scaffold a manifest and an adapter detecting one to report an install must not disagree about one
project — and it uses `fs.Lstat` for the reason `init` uses `Lstat`: the question is whether the
harness left something behind, not whether it resolves. A rule installs as a standalone file the
harness discovers on its own, and nothing references it from `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` or a managed
block; the adapter can add no such reference because a destination is the whole of its answer.

Adapter packages self-register from their own `init` and `cmd/harnaas/cli/adapters.go` is the one
file where linking them is decided, exactly as `sourcekinds.go` is for source kinds. The import
boundary is a test rather than a linter rule, because it is a property of this directory rather than
of the module: an adapter may reach the contract, the roster and the manifest vocabulary, and
nothing else — not the install flow, which imports *it*. Go permits that import right up until the
cycle closes, so the test is what makes the failure arrive while it is still one import.
